newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian cotton crop seen cut by rain.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian cotton crop seen cut by rain.

text.p: Further heavy rain and localised flooding in northern New South Wales (NSW) was likely to reduce Australia's 1996/97 cotton crop, traders and industry sources said on Monday.

The early consensus after a further weekend of rain is that the crop is now likely to amount to about 2.4 million 500-pound bales, down from the Australian Bureau of Agricultural and Resource Economics (ABARE) forecast of 2.5 million bales.

With the Namoi and Gwydir valleys in northern New South Wales (NSW) flooded, leaving crops waterlogged and water with nowhere to go at present, picking of the crop would be delayed at the least, industry sources told Reuters.
The Gwydir and Namoi valleys produce about 40 percent of Australia's cotton crop.
David Lindsay, Wee Waa-based manager grower services of Namoi Cotton Co-operative, told Reuters on Friday that heavy rain and flooding was likely to produce a harvest of about 2.4 million bales.
A spokeswoman for Goondiwindi-based Cotton Trading Corp on Monday said while assessments were still in progress, there was a "strong possibility" that the crop could be reduced to 2.4 million bales.
Information was still being gathered, she said.
Sydney Futures Exchange broker Brendan Hillary, of ANZ Futures Ltd, said if the rain did not stop it would have an effect.
Damage so far was minimal but a crop reduction to 2.4 million bales was possible, he said.
A well-placed cotton source in Moree, in the flooded Gwydir valley, said the industry was tipping lower production than forecast for the 1996/97 crop.

Much would depend on weather in the next two to three weeks. Sunny weather could quickly restore the crop to a more normal condition, but one with only average yields on a delayed harvest, said the source, who asked not to be identified.
Localised flooding had been caused by the weekend rain following earlier significant rain of 10 days to two weeks ago.
Most cotton crops were protected by levee banks and damage would be minimal but the extended wet season would be highly likely to produce only average yields.
Results would not be known for about two weeks, the source said.
The Gwydir valley is expected to produce about 650,000 bales this season, or about 25 percent of Australia's cotton crop, estimated to be worth a total of about A$1.1 billion.
Other cotton-growing areas in southern Queensland beyond the Namoi and Gwydir valleys have not been affected by rains and flooding to the same extent as the NSW areas.
Cotton picking normally begins in late March and early April in the Gwydir valley. Even before the rain, a start to picking was expected to be delayed this year by three weeks.

Weather in the Gwydir valley on Monday morning was fine but tropical cyclone Harold was 1,300 km east of Cooktown, north of Cairns off the Queensland coast travelling southwest at about 15 nautical knots an hour. The Queensland Bureau of Meteorology said Harold was not expected to touch land.
The Australian Cotton Foundation was still assessing the crop situation when contacted by Reuters on Monday.
-- Michael Byrnes, Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
